extracted.intended_audience: readers (and writers) of humorous detective short fiction / anyone studying detective-story tropes
extracted.subtask_description: A humorous early-20th-century detective short story (Philo Gubb) mixing slapstick, detective 'lessons', and tropes like disguises, expert identification, and sensational dime-novel methods. Useful for writers studying detective-craft tropes in comic fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to detail / 'complicity of detail'
rubrics_metrics.description: "The deteckative profession is full of complicity of detail ... and the impossible is quite possible when put in the right hands."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, specific details can solve cases; the profession depends on noticing particulars (tattoos, marks, bits of recovered property). The narrative shows Philo's clue-driven thinking (tattoo claws -> possible identity). Anti-pattern: ignoring small marks or facts that later prove decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of disguise
rubrics_metrics.description: List of disguises and the need to choose one suited to the work (Number Seven, Card Sharp; Number Nine, Minister of the Gospel; Number Twelve, Butcher; Number Sixteen, Negro Hack-Driver; Number Seventeen, Chinese Laundryman; Number Twenty, Cowboy ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a disguise appropriate to the situation and whether you want to be seen or remain unseen. Example: Philo chooses 'cowboy' because it is a 'jaunty disguise' and he wants to 'see and be seen by Syrilla.' Anti-pattern: using an ill-fitting disguise that draws unintended attention or fails to match the role needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to be seen vs. unseen
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ordinarily Mr. Gubb would have taken any disguise that seemed to him best suited for the work in hand; but now he was going to see and be seen by Syrilla!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical choice: sometimes a detective disguises to blend in and observe unnoticed; other times the disguise should invite recognition (to interact with a subject). Match visibility to investigative goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert identification (tattoo/handwriting analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Gubb: 'if he could prove that the claws tattooed on Syrilla's arm were the work of Mr. Schreckenheim, his case would be complete' — analogous to consulting a handwriting expert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corroborative expert testimony (tattoo artist, handwriting expert) is a method to link marks to a particular source/person. Example: seeking Mr. Enderbury or Schreckenheim to identify tattoo work. Anti-pattern: relying on single-eye judgment without expert corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstantial evidence and inference from silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Gubb: 'I consider that conclusive circumstantial evidence that they are,' referring to Enderbury's refusal to speak as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silence or refusal to answer by a knowledgeable witness may be used as circumstantial evidence, but it's inferential and not absolute; the story treats such silence as strongly probative. Caveat: be cautious—silence can have many causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lesson One — fearlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first words in Lesson One is these: 'The deteckative must be a man devoid of fear.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional expectation (in the parody) that a detective must accept danger and not be deterred by threats. Illustrated by Philo continuing despite being beaten and threatened. Anti-pattern: allowing fear to halt investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lesson Four / Rules on working and trailing in the dark
rubrics_metrics.description: "Lesson Four says--I got to proceed cautiously when workin' in the dark." and references to 'Lesson Four, Rules Four to Seventeen' concerning picking up suspicious persons and trailing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When surveilling (especially at night) proceed cautiously; trailing has explicit rules (multiple rules invoked) — practice stealth, patience, and procedural care. Example: Philo hides in doorways, picks up suspicious people, then attempts to shadow them. Anti-patterns: sloppy trailing that results in being beaten or led astray (as happens to Philo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence / perfection in recovery work
rubrics_metrics.description: Motto: 'Perfection, no matter how many times.' (applied to recovering stolen property — Philo recovers the cup twice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional standard of persistence and thoroughness: recover and verify success even if it requires repeating work. Value placed on achieving the goal regardless of repetition or inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of criminal methods (caution about sensational sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philo reads 'The Pale Avengers' dime novel which dramatizes methods like the oubliette; the story shows how sensational fiction can shape a detective's fears/expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning about criminal methods from literature can broaden imagination of possible threats (e.g., oubliette), but it can also instill exaggerated fears or unrealistic expectations. Use such sources critically; corroborate with real-world knowledge rather than letting fiction dictate tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social engineering / leverage (offers, bargains, and using promises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Gubb uses the promise of a wealthy home and reward to persuade Syrilla; Mr. Medderbrook negotiates reward payment methods (stock vs. cash).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative tactics can include leveraging offers or promises to elicit cooperation or testimony. Also be mindful of the form of rewards/compensation (cash vs. stock) and the practical consequences. Anti-pattern: accepting dubious or non-liquid compensation without understanding terms.
